newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt police arrest 150 at protest over farm law.
newsitem.headline: Egypt police arrest 150 at protest over farm law.

text.p: Egyptian police arrested 150 people for demonstrating against a new farm land law and burning a government building on Wednesday, security sources said.

The demonstrators set fire to the farm cooperative society in a village near the Nile Delta town of Mahalla el-Kubra, 120 km (75 miles) north of Cairo, after officials had refused to provide them with agricultural supplies, the sources said.
No one was reported hurt in the incidents.
The new law takes effect in October. It stops tenants from passing their leases automatically to their inheritors, generation after generation. It also deregulates the rent on agricultural land.
The sources quoted protesters as saying the farm cooperative said it has received instructions from the agriculture minister to stop selling tenants supplies from July 1.
The sources have said cooperative societies have instructions to start procedures for transferring possession documents from tenants to land-owners.
Three people were killed and dozens of farm tenant demonstrators were arrested in southern Egypt on Tuesday when police broke up a riot by farmers to protest the law.
Security sources said the prosecutor's office ordered them detained for 15 days and charged them with rioting, wasting public money and resisting the authorities.
The new law, and other recently introduced bills, scraps many provisions installed by the late socialist president Gamal Abdel-Nasser in the late 1950s.
The current law makes it almost impossible for land-owners to sell their land without splitting the price with tenants.
Interior Minister Hassan el-Alfi told reporters last month that the government would not change its mind about the new law and that security forces would deal firmly with any trouble.
The government has said it would provide reclaimed land to tenants who lose leases once the law comes into effect.

Opponents of the law have brushed this aside, saying there would not be enough land for all and that the formerly desert land would need a lot of work to become as fertile as the land they used to tend.
